summary: Analyzes spam in SIP, where any user-to-user system can be abused. It considers how the problem is similar to and different from email spam and examines possible solutions. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Junk mail can also show up as junk phone calls over the internet. This looks at why and what could help.

questions: how to prevent spam over ip telephony
what is spam over sip networks
subtitle: Spam in voice and presence communications over SIP

tldr.problem: The Session Initiation Protocol enables user-to-user voice, video, and instant messaging, making it subject to spam just like email. SIP spam differs from email spam in key ways and requires tailored solutions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes three types of SIP spam (call spam, IM spam, presence spam), examines email anti-spam techniques for applicability to SIP, and proposes a framework combining strong identity, white lists, and introduction mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: No single solution eliminates SIP spam, but a layered approach using SIP Identity, white/black lists, and consent-based communications can significantly reduce the problem.

today: RFC 5039 remains an influential analysis of SIP spam and security. While SIP adoption has been more limited than anticipated in the early 2000s, the framework and recommendations remain relevant. The document helped establish SIP Identity as a key requirement for secure inter-domain SIP communications and informed the development of consent-based frameworks and presence authorization in later standards.

sections.title: The Problem Space
sections.content:
Email spam is well-established as a serious problem, but spam is not limited to email. Any system enabling user-to-user communication can be targeted for spam. The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) is used for multimedia communications including voice, video, instant messaging, and presence information.

This document analyzes spam in SIP by examining how email anti-spam techniques apply, considering the unique characteristics of SIP, and making recommendations for implementors and network operators. The analysis is based on cost modeling, protocol mechanics, and the lessons learned from email spam.
sections.plainLanguage: Email got spam, so phone calls and instant messages over the internet will too. We need to understand the problem and steal good ideas from email but adapt them for phones.

sections.title: Three Types of SIP Spam
sections.content:
Call Spam (SPIT): Bulk unsolicited INVITE requests attempting to establish a voice or video session. If the recipient answers, the spammer plays a recorded announcement. This mimics traditional telemarketer calls but is dramatically cheaper to execute. A simple SIP user agent can send parallel calls using low-end PC hardware and a broadband connection. Cost analysis shows SIP call spam is roughly four orders of magnitude cheaper than traditional circuit-based telemarketing: traditional calls cost about 250,000 microcents per successful delivery, while SIP calls over a typical broadband connection cost about 6.22 microcents.

IM Spam (SPIM): Bulk unsolicited instant messages, similar to email spam. These can be sent using the SIP MESSAGE request. The cost is within a small factor of IM spam, roughly 0.31 microcents per message. Like email spam, content filtering tools can be applied, though IM is more intrusive because messages pop up automatically.

Presence Spam (SPPP): Bulk unsolicited SUBSCRIBE requests for presence information. These are meant to get on a user's buddy list or white list to enable follow-up spam. However, presence systems typically notify users of presence requests, allowing the user to approve or deny them. Spammers can exploit this by encoding brief messages in the subscribe request URI itself, using sender identities like sip:please-buy-my-product@spam.example.com to convey information.
sections.plainLanguage: Junk calls use INVITE (hey, pick up). Junk messages use MESSAGE (check this out). Junk subscription requests use SUBSCRIBE (let me see your status). All three exist because they're cheap to send and hard to block.

sections.title: Anti-Spam Techniques
sections.content:
Content Filtering: Works for IM spam (like email filtering) but fails for call spam. Speech and video recognition technology is insufficient to detect spam automatically before the user experiences the call. Content filtering is ineffective against sophisticated spammers.

Black and White Lists: Black lists (lists of known spammers) are ineffective because identities are easy to spoof and manufacture. White lists (lists of approved senders) work better but create the introduction problem: how does a legitimate new contact get on the white list? White lists are most effective when they correspond to existing buddy lists in IM systems, which users maintain for other purposes.

Consent-Based Communications: A requester who is not on a white or black list receives an initial rejection and must request consent. On the recipient's next login, they are informed of the request and can approve or deny it. This framework, standardized in SIP for presence using the watcher information event package, can reduce spam at the cost of annoying users with consent requests instead of spam. Some of these requests themselves convey spam (via the requester's URI identity), though content filtering can mitigate this.

Reputation Systems: Systems where accumulated feedback determines a user's reputation. Negative reputation (users report bad behavior) suffers from the same blacklist problems. Positive reputation (users praise good behavior) is more effective but vulnerable to collectives of spammers praising each other. Reputation systems work best in centralized networks with strong identity and can be enhanced by leveraging existing buddy lists as automated praise.

Turing Tests and Computational Puzzles: Turing tests (CAPTCHA-like challenges) can be adapted to voice, but spammers can use cheap labor to solve them (costing about 0.50 cents per test). Computational puzzles increase the cost of sending spam but are bypassed when spammers use virus-infected machines (zombies) with substantial computational power.

Payments at Risk: The sender deposits a small amount of money with the recipient. If the recipient determines the message is legitimate, they refund it; otherwise they keep it. This could make spam arbitrarily expensive but requires micro-payment infrastructure. At very small amounts (1-5 cents), transaction costs become significant.

Legal Action: Countries can pass anti-spam laws. However, international spam from jurisdictions where legal action is impractical limits effectiveness, unlike the more effective US do not call list which applies primarily to domestic telemarketing.

Circles of Trust and Centralized Providers: Domains can form agreements to police spam from their users and fine violators. Alternatively, a few centralized inter-domain providers could monopolize inter-domain traffic and charge per-message fees. These work but reintroduce the centralized complexity that SIP aims to avoid.
sections.plainLanguage: Block known bad actors (doesn't work, too many). Trust your buddies (works but new people are blocked). Ask permission (works but people get annoyed). Watch someone's reputation (works unless spammers help each other). Make solvers prove they're human (spammers hire cheap workers). Charge money (works but needs tiny payments). Pass laws (only works in your country). Create networks of trusted providers (works but defeats the purpose).

sections.title: Authenticated Identity
sections.content:
Many anti-spam techniques depend on strong identity authentication. In email, this is provided by mechanisms like Sender ID and DKIM signatures, which verify that a message actually comes from the domain it claims to originate from.

SIP provides the SIP Identity mechanism (RFC 4474) for strong inter-domain authenticated identity. A domain authenticates its own users (typically using TLS-protected digest authentication), then signs assertions about user identity when relaying messages to other domains. This is stronger than the P-Asserted-Identity header, which requires mutual trust among all domains and becomes ineffective when the chain includes untrustworthy domains.

SIP also supports TLS with mutual authentication between domains, allowing one domain to verify it is communicating with a legitimate representative of another domain.
sections.plainLanguage: If routers sign messages with their private keys, you know the message really came from that router. Email uses signatures too. SIP has the same idea for phone calls.

sections.title: Recommended Framework
sections.content:
No single magic bullet solves SIP spam. Instead, a layered framework is recommended:

Strong Identity: Network operators should deploy SIP Identity (RFC 4474) to authenticate senders across domain boundaries. P-Asserted-Identity is insufficient because its effectiveness depends on the weakest link in the chain.

White Lists: Networks should use white lists, ideally built from existing buddy lists. Users who are added to a white list are guaranteed by identity authentication.

Introduction Mechanisms: One or more mechanisms should be used to solve the introduction problem, allowing new contacts to be added to white lists. These might include consent frameworks, Turing tests, computational puzzles, or reputation systems. Users completing an introduction can be automatically added to the white list.

Don't Wait: Most critically, providers should not ignore the spam problem until it becomes widespread. As soon as a provider interconnects with others or accepts messages from the open internet, they must consider spam mitigation strategies.

Providers should monitor how anti-spam techniques evolve in the email space and adapt the best ideas for SIP.
sections.plainLanguage: Use strong signatures so you know who's sending. Keep a buddy list. Ask permission when meeting someone new and have them prove they're human. Deal with spam now, not when you're drowning in it.
